content:
"The night had started like any other for Dale Scott Walkinshaw. The 23-year-old had gone out to a Darwin bar, looking to forget his troubles for a few hours. He'd met a young woman there, and they'd hit it off over drinks – too many drinks, as it would turn out. When they left together in his Toyota Hilux, Walkinshaw was in no condition to drive, but judgment had long since abandoned him.

The crash at the corner of Stuart Highway and Bargot Road was violent. The palm tree stopped the vehicle cold, and Walkinshaw's passenger bore the brunt of it. As he held her behind the vegetation, watching her drift in and out of consciousness, he knew he'd crossed a line he could never uncross. The sirens approaching only confirmed what he already knew – his life was about to change forever.

The two officers who discovered them had been on their way to something routine, a noise complaint. Instead, they found Walkinshaw cradling the injured woman, reeking of alcohol, his blood alcohol reading nearly three times the legal limit. They arrested him and placed him in the back of the caged police vehicle.

What happened next would become the subject of Coroner Greg Cavanagh's scathing report. Alone in the cage, overwhelmed by guilt and fear, Walkinshaw attempted to take his own life. He wasn't the first – he was one of at least 16 people who had tried the same thing in NT police vehicles over the previous three years. Six of them had nearly succeeded, found only when they were already unconscious.

The officers didn't notice until it was too late. There were no cameras in the cage, despite an internal report from 2013 – following another death in custody – that had recommended their installation. The report had gathered dust while vulnerable people continued to harm themselves in those mobile cells, invisible to the officers driving them.

Walkinshaw became another statistic, another preventable death that highlighted systemic failures in the Northern Territory police force. His death certificate would read September 16, but the truth was that his fate had been sealed years earlier, when bureaucracy and indifference conspired to ignore a simple recommendation that could have saved his life and others.

Coroner Cavanagh's findings were damning: 'It wasn't a matter of if a person would die in the back of a police van but when.' The prediction had been horrifyingly accurate. Dale Scott Walkinshaw, guilty of a terrible mistake but deserving of better care, had become the 'when.'

The young woman he'd injured that night survived, though she would carry the physical and emotional scars forever. She would learn of Walkinshaw's death weeks later, adding another layer of trauma to an already devastating experience. The crash had claimed two victims that night – one immediately, one a few hours later in the back of a police van that had become a death trap.

The coroner's report would recommend, once again, the installation of CCTV cameras in all caged police vehicles. Whether this recommendation would be acted upon, or whether it would join its 2013 predecessor in gathering dust, remained to be seen. What was certain was that Dale Scott Walkinshaw's death was preventable, a tragedy born of systemic negligence that had been documented, reported, and ignored."
